title: Milestones
blurb: State the purpose of milestones: zero-duration markers for progress, focus, key dates, decisions and payments.
question: The sponsor of a new community library wants a one-page view of when the big things will be achieved, and the building contractor wants to be paid in stages. Which schedule feature serves both needs, and what is its purpose?

teach.body: A milestone is a significant event in the schedule. It has zero duration: it marks a moment, such as 'design approved' or 'building handed over', rather than a piece of work. Milestones usually mark the completion of a key deliverable, the end of a phase or a decision point. The work to get there is shown by activities; the milestone is the flag at the finish line.

teach.caption: Bars are work that takes time. Diamonds are moments: they take no time and use no resources.

teach.body: Formally, a milestone is a key event in a project schedule, with zero duration, typically marking the completion of a significant deliverable, phase or decision. Plainly: a checkpoint you either have or haven't reached. That yes-or-no quality is what makes milestones so useful for tracking, communicating and paying for progress.

teach.caption: Senior stakeholders rarely need every activity; a milestone summary gives them the key dates.

items: Set milestones at meaningful points: deliverables complete, phases end, decisions due.
Report planned, forecast and actual dates for each one.
A milestone forecast to be late is an early warning of slippage: act on it.
Because a milestone is either achieved or not, it's harder to overstate than '80% done'.
Use milestones as gate and approval points, and link supplier payments to them.

teach.body: At Westfield, the contractor is paid when 'building handed over' is achieved, not simply because nine months have passed. Linking staged payments to milestones means the client pays for results. Likewise, the 'design approved' milestone is a decision point: the board confirms the design before construction money is committed.

teach.text: A milestone has ZERO duration. Options describing it as 'a short activity', 'a phase' or 'the period of work to produce a deliverable' are wrong. And a milestone is not the deliverable itself: it marks the moment the deliverable is completed or approved.

items: Milestone: a significant event in the schedule with zero duration.
Usually marks completion of a key deliverable, a phase or a decision point.
Purposes: monitoring and reporting checkpoints, team focus, communicating key dates, decision and payment points.
Shown as a diamond on a Gantt chart; uses no time or resources.
A missed or late milestone is an early warning of slippage.

summary: You can now define a milestone as a zero-duration event marking a significant point in the schedule, and state its purposes: checkpoints for monitoring and reporting, focus for the team, key dates for stakeholders, and decision and payment points.

A.q: What is the duration of a milestone?
A.why: A milestone marks a point in time, so it has zero duration.

whyNot.0: Anything lasting a day is an activity, not a milestone.
whyNot.2: A phase has duration; a milestone may mark its end.
whyNot.3: Reporting periods are time intervals; milestones are moments.

A.q: Which of the following best describes a milestone?
options: A significant event marking an achievement
A short activity at the end of each phase
A period of work producing a deliverable
A reserve of time held for late activities
A.why: A milestone is a significant, zero-duration event, such as completing a key deliverable or reaching a decision point.

whyNot.1: A milestone is not an activity of any length.
whyNot.2: Work producing a deliverable is an activity; the milestone marks its completion.
whyNot.3: A time reserve is contingency or a buffer, not a milestone.

A.q:
Which TWO are purposes of milestones?
1. Checkpoints for monitoring progress
2. Calculating activity float
3. Communicating key dates to stakeholders
4. Assigning work to team members
A.why: Milestones act as checkpoints for monitoring progress and communicate key dates to stakeholders.

whyNot.0: Float comes from critical path analysis, not from milestones.
whyNot.1: Neither calculating float nor assigning work is a purpose of milestones.
whyNot.2: Assigning work to people is done through the RAM, not milestones.

B.q: A building contract says the client will pay the contractor when 'roof complete' is achieved. Which purpose of a milestone does this show?
B.why: Milestones are often used as payment points, so suppliers are paid for achievements rather than elapsed time.

whyNot.0: Float is flexibility in the schedule, not a payment trigger.
whyNot.1: A resource limit is about availability, not paying a supplier.
whyNot.3: A risk response is an action to address a risk, not a payment trigger.

B.q: How does a milestone help the project team stay focused?
options: It removes the need for detailed plans
It guarantees the work is high quality
It gives a clear near-term target
It fixes the budget for the next stage
B.why: A visible, near-term milestone gives the team something concrete to aim for and celebrate, which builds focus and motivation.

whyNot.0: Detailed plans are still needed to reach each milestone.
whyNot.1: Quality comes from quality planning and control, not from a milestone.
whyNot.3: Budgets are set through planning and governance, not by milestones.

B.q: How is a milestone normally shown on a Gantt chart?
B.why: Because it has zero duration, a milestone is drawn as a diamond (or similar symbol) at a single point in time.

whyNot.1: A bar represents an activity with duration.
whyNot.2: A dotted or outlined tail usually shows float.

C.q: A governance board will decide whether to continue once the 'business case refreshed' milestone is reached. Which purpose is the milestone serving?
C.why: Milestones often mark decision or approval points, such as a stage gate where the board decides whether to proceed.

whyNot.0: Float is not marked by milestones.
whyNot.1: Lessons are recorded in a lessons log, not by a milestone.
whyNot.2: Quality tests are activities with duration, not milestones.

C.q: Which of the following would NOT make a sensible milestone?
C.why: Preparing documents is work that takes time, so it is an activity. The others are zero-duration events.

whyNot.0: Permission being granted is a significant moment: a good milestone.
whyNot.2: Signing a contract is a key event and decision point: a good milestone.
whyNot.3: Handover marks completion of a key deliverable: a good milestone.

C.q: A supplier reports every task as '80% done', yet no milestones have been reached. Why might the PM prefer to track milestones?
options: Achieved-or-not events are hard to overstate
Milestones remove the need for a schedule
Milestones measure the cost of each activity
Milestones show how much float is left
C.why: A milestone is either achieved or not, so it gives an objective checkpoint, unlike a percentage complete that can be optimistic.

whyNot.1: Milestones sit within the schedule; they don't replace it.
whyNot.2: Milestones have zero duration and no cost of their own.
whyNot.3: Float comes from critical path analysis, not milestones.

reteach.title: Think of a long car journey
reteach.question: You're driving from London to Edinburgh with the family. How do you, and the people waiting for you, know how the trip is going?

blocks.body: You don't track every mile; you watch for big moments: 'past Birmingham', 'lunch stop at York', 'crossed the border'. Each one takes no time at all, you've either passed it or you haven't. Hitting them keeps everyone going, missing one tells you you're running late, and texting 'just passed York' tells the relatives when to put the kettle on.
Project milestones do the same: zero-duration checkpoints that show progress, motivate the team, tell stakeholders the key dates and mark where decisions or payments happen.

explain.body: A milestone marks a single point in time. It contains no work and uses no resources, which is why it has zero duration and appears as a diamond, not a bar.

test.q: Why does a milestone have zero duration?
options: Its work is all done by suppliers
Its float has all been used up
It marks a moment, not any work
test.why: A milestone represents an event at a point in time; the work leading to it sits in activities.

whyNot.0: Who does the work doesn't affect the milestone's duration.
whyNot.1: Milestones can be achieved early, on time or late.
whyNot.2: Float has nothing to do with milestone duration.

explain.body: Comparing planned and actual milestone dates is a simple, objective way to see whether a project is on track. A milestone forecast to be late is an early warning to act.

test.q: Comparing planned and forecast milestone dates mainly helps the project manager to do what?
test.why: A gap between planned and forecast milestone dates warns that the project is slipping, so corrective action can be taken early.

whyNot.0: Budget approval is a governance decision.
whyNot.1: Supplier selection follows the procurement strategy.
whyNot.3: Quality standards come from the quality plan.

explain.body: Stakeholders want key dates, not every task. A milestone summary gives them that. For the team, reaching a milestone is a visible achievement that builds momentum.

test.q: Why might a PM give the board a schedule showing only milestones?
options: The board must approve every task
It shows key dates without the detail
It hides any delays from the board
Milestones cost far less to plan
test.why: A milestone summary communicates the key dates senior stakeholders need, without the detail of every activity.

whyNot.0: Boards approve key decisions, not every task.
whyNot.2: Milestone reports should reveal delays, not hide them.
whyNot.3: Cost of planning is not the reason; clarity is.

explain.body: Milestones are natural places for decisions (such as a gate review) and for staged payments to suppliers, so money is released for results rather than for time passing.

test.q: Linking supplier payments to milestones mainly ensures the client does what?
options: Pays for results, not time passing
Pays the whole sum in advance
Takes on all the supplier's risk
test.why: Milestone-based payments release money only when agreed achievements are reached.

whyNot.1: Milestone payments are staged, not paid up front.
whyNot.2: A contract is still needed to set out the milestones and payments.
whyNot.3: Milestone payments tend to reduce the client's risk, not increase it.
